We need to propose a retrosynthesis route (max 3 steps) to target SMILES: Cc1ccc(NS(=O)(=O)c2ccc(/C=C/C(=O)Nc3ccccc3N)cc2)cc1

We need leaves commercially available, total price <= $9999. Need to find templates for disconnections.

We can think of disconnections: The molecule has a sulfonamide linking two aromatic rings: a tolyl sulfonyl attached to a phenyl ring bearing a trans-α,β-unsaturated amide (C= C - C(=O)N-Ph-NH2). So we can disconnect at sulfonamide bond (S-N) to get tolyl sulfonyl chloride (or sulfonic acid) and an aniline (the other aromatic ring with the side chain). Also disconnect the amide formation between the α,β-unsaturated acid (cinnamic acid derivative) and an aniline (anilide). So two steps: 1) sulfonyl chloride + aniline coupling to give sulfonamide. 2) amide coupling between cinnamic acid (or its activated derivative) and aniline (the second aromatic). The side chain includes trans-alkene; could be formed via Wittig or Heck coupling, but maybe we can use commercially available trans-cinnamic acid derivative with amide.

Simplify: Use commercially available 4-(methyl)aniline (p-toluidine) as starting for sulfonyl chloride? Actually we need p-tolyl sulfonyl chloride (p-toluenesulfonyl chloride, TsCl) is cheap and commercial. Then we need the other aromatic amine: 4-((E)-3-(phenylamino)acryloyl)aniline? Wait the other aromatic is phenyl ring with amide attached to trans-alkene and also an aniline substituent (NH2) at para? Let's parse: c2ccc(/C=C/C(=O)Nc3ccccc3N)cc2 is a phenyl ring (ring B) with a para substituent? Actually the SMILES: c2ccc(/C=C/C(=O)Nc3ccccc3N)cc2 indicates a phenyl ring with a side chain at position 1 (maybe para). The side chain is /C=C/C(=O)N-Ph-NH2 (cinnamoyl anilide). So the phenyl ring B is attached to sulfonyl group via its para position? The sulfonyl attaches to the nitrogen of sulfonamide, not to the ring. So the sulfonamide nitrogen is attached to the tolyl ring (p-methyl phenyl). The other side of sulfonamide is attached to the phenyl ring B (the same as the aromatic ring bearing the side chain). Actually the SMILES: NS(=O)(=O)c2ccc(... )cc2 indicates the sulfonamide nitrogen attached to the phenyl ring B (the sulfonyl attached to that phenyl). So the sulfonamide is attached to phenyl B (para to side chain). So the sulfonamide nitrogen is attached to phenyl B, not to tolyl. Wait: The SMILES: Cc1ccc(NS(=O)(=O)c2ccc(... )cc2)cc1. So tolyl ring (ring A) has substituent NS(=O)(=O) attached to it (the N attached to tolyl). The sulfonyl group attaches to phenyl B. So the sulfonamide nitrogen is attached to tolyl ring, and the sulfonyl attached to phenyl B. So we have tolyl sulfonyl chloride reacting with aniline (phenyl B with side chain) to give sulfonamide.

Thus step 1: sulfonyl chloride (p-toluenesulfonyl chloride, TsCl) + aniline (the phenyl B with side chain) -> target.

Step 2: The aniline (phenyl B with side chain) can be made via amide coupling of trans-cinnamic acid (or its activated derivative) with 4-aminophenyl? Actually the side chain is C(=O)N-Ph-NH2 where the amide nitrogen attached to phenyl c3ccccc3N (an aniline). So the amide is between cinnamic acid and aniline (aniline is 4-aminophenyl? Wait the phenyl attached to amide is c3ccccc3N (aniline). That's a phenyl ring with an NH2 at para? Actually c3ccccc3N is an aniline (aniline). No substituents else. So the amide is between cinnamic acid and aniline (aniline is attached to carbonyl). So we need to attach aniline to cinnamic acid via amide bond. The cinnamic acid is trans-3-phenylacrylic acid (cinnamic acid). So we need to couple cinnamic acid with aniline to give trans-cinnamoyl anilide (C(=O)N-Ph). That's step 2.

Thus overall 2 steps: 1) amide formation (cinnamic acid + aniline) -> intermediate (cinnamoyl aniline). 2) sulfonylation of that aniline (the aniline is the same as the one used? Wait the aniline used in amide is the same as the phenyl attached to amide (c3ccccc3N). That aniline after amide still has NH2? Actually after amide, the aniline nitrogen is part of amide, not free. The free amine is on the phenyl B (the one attached to sulfonyl). Wait we have two aniline nitrogens: one is the sulfonamide nitrogen attached to tolyl; the other is the aniline attached to carbonyl (amide). The phenyl B has the sulfonamide nitrogen attached (as N-sulfonyl) and also the side chain (cinnamoyl anilide) attached at para? Actually the phenyl B is attached to sulfonyl via S, not via N. The SMILES: NS(=O)(=O)c2ccc(... )cc2. So the phenyl B is attached to sulfonyl via S, not via N. The sulfonamide nitrogen is attached to tolyl ring. So the phenyl B is a sulfonyl aryl group (aryl sulfonyl). The side chain is attached to phenyl B via a carbon (the aromatic carbon). So the phenyl B has two substituents: the sulfonyl group (attached via S) and the side chain (attached via carbon). So the aniline used for amide is not part of phenyl B; it's a separate phenyl (c3ccccc3N) attached to carbonyl. So the amide uses aniline (aniline) as nucleophile, giving N-phenyl amide. That aniline is separate and remains as an aniline (has NH2). So the final product has an aniline attached to carbonyl (C(=O)N-Ph-NH2). So the aniline is free NH2 on that phenyl.

Thus the intermediate after step 2 (amide) is: trans-cinnamoyl aniline (C6H5-NH-CO-CH=CH-Ph). This molecule has a free NH2 on the aniline? Wait the aniline is the N attached to carbonyl, so its NH is part of amide (no free NH2). The SMILES: C(=O)N c3ccccc3N indicates carbonyl attached to N which is attached to phenyl that also has an NH2 substituent? Actually "Nc3ccccc3N" means N attached to phenyl which also has an N? Let's parse: C(=O)N c3ccccc3N: The carbonyl attached to N, which is attached to phenyl ring that has an N substituent (aniline). So the amide nitrogen is attached to phenyl that also has an NH2 substituent (para?). So the phenyl ring c3ccccc3N is an aniline (has NH2). So the amide nitrogen is attached to the phenyl carbon (i.e., N-aryl amide). So the phenyl ring has an NH2 substituent (free). So the amide is N-aryl amide where the aryl has an NH2 group. So we need to start from 4-aminophenyl (p-aminophenyl) as the aryl amine for amide formation? Actually the amide nitrogen is attached to the phenyl carbon, not to the NH2. So the amide is formed between cinnamic acid and aniline (aniline is the nucleophile). The product is N-phenylcinnamamide, which has a phenyl attached to nitrogen. That phenyl has an NH2 substituent (para). So the starting aniline is 4-aminophenyl (p-aminophenyl) which after amide becomes N-(4-aminophenyl) cinnamamide. So the free NH2 remains on that phenyl.

Thus step 2: cinnamic acid + 4-aminophenyl (p-phenylenediamine? Actually p-aminophenyl is aniline with NH2 at para? That's p-phenylenediamine has two NH2 groups. But we need a phenyl with one NH2 (para to the amide attachment). The amide attaches at the carbon of phenyl (i.e., the phenyl is attached via its carbon to N). That's typical for anilide: the nitrogen attaches to carbonyl, not to phenyl carbon. So the phenyl is attached to nitrogen, not the other way. So the amide nitrogen is attached to phenyl carbon (i.e., N-aryl). The phenyl has an NH2 substituent at para position relative to the N-aryl bond. So the starting material is 4-aminophenylamine? Actually we need a phenyl with an NH2 substituent, and we need to attach the amide nitrogen to the phenyl carbon (i.e., the phenyl is attached to nitrogen). That's just aniline (Ph-NH2) reacting with cinnamic acid to give N-phenylcinnamamide (Ph-NH-CO-CH=CH-Ph). That product does not have an extra NH2. So the SMILES would be O=C(Nc1ccc(N)cc1)/C=C/c2ccccc2. Indeed that's our side chain: C(=O)N c3ccccc3N where the phenyl has an NH2 substituent. So the phenyl is aniline with an NH2 at para? Actually the SMILES "Nc3ccccc3N" indicates an aniline where the nitrogen attached to carbonyl is attached to the phenyl at position 1, and there is another N attached to the phenyl at position 1? Wait "Nc3ccccc3N" means N attached to aromatic carbon (position 1) and also the aromatic carbon has an N attached (i.e., an aniline). That's ambiguous. Let's generate: "Nc1ccccc1N" is a phenyl with two NH substituents at positions 1 and maybe 1? Actually both N attached to same carbon? That would be impossible. So maybe the SMILES is "Nc3ccccc3N" meaning an aniline where the nitrogen attached to carbonyl is attached to the aromatic carbon (makes N-aryl), and the aromatic also has an NH2 substituent at another position (maybe para). The SMILES would be "N(c1ccc(N)cc1)"? Actually typical SMILES for N-(4-aminophenyl) cinnamamide: "O=C(Nc1ccc(N)cc1)/C=C/c2ccccc2". That matches our side chain: C(=O)N c3ccccc3N with the aromatic having an NH2. So we need 4-aminophenylamine? That's p-phenylenediamine (1,4-diaminobenzene). The amide attaches to one amine, leaving the other free. So starting material could be p-phenylenediamine (commercial) and cinnamic acid (commercial). Then we need selective acylation of one amine, leaving the other free. That is feasible using protecting group (e.g., Boc) then deprotect. But we have only 3 steps total. Could we avoid protection by using stoichiometric control? Might be okay.

Thus route: Step 1: Acylate p-phenylenediamine with cinnamic acid (using coupling reagent like EDC/HCl) to give N-(4-aminophenyl) cinnamamide (intermediate). Step 2: Sulfonylate the free amine (the other NH2) with p-toluenesulfonyl chloride to give final product. That's 2 steps.

Leaves: p-toluenesulfonyl chloride (TsCl) and p-phenylenediamine and trans-cinnamic acid. All commercially available and cheap (<$100 each). Total cost well under $9999.

We need to provide JSON with reaction nodes and template IDs. We need to find template IDs for sulfonylation of aniline with sulfonyl chloride, and amide coupling of carboxylic acid with amine.

Search for amide formation template: Use functional_groups_formed "amide". Let's search.
